resources.string: Silver birch
Betula pendula
Bouleau verruqueux
White bark, dark and fissured at the base of older trunks. Slender, often drooping twigs bear small warts. Triangular leaves and tiny winged fruits.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Common alder
Alnus glutinosa
Aulne glutineux
Rounded leaves, often notched at the tip. Long hanging male catkins; woody female fruiting structures resemble small cones, but this is not a conifer.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Horse chestnut
Aesculus hippocastanum
Marronnier d’Inde
Opposite leaves with 5–7 large leaflets meeting at one point. Upright flower panicles. Sparsely spiny capsules contain one or a few large seeds.
Native to the Balkans; widely planted in French parks and avenues.
Silver fir
Abies alba
Sapin pectiné
Flat, usually blunt needles with two pale bands underneath. Upright cones break apart on the tree, leaving their central axis behind.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Common box
Buxus sempervirens
Buis commun
Small opposite leathery leaves with rounded or slightly notched tips. Yellowish flowers without petals in leaf axils. Capsules end in three small points.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Common daisy
Bellis perennis
Pâquerette vivace
All leaves form a spoon-leaved basal rosette. Each leafless stalk carries one head: white, sometimes pink, ray florets surround yellow tubular florets.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Common yarrow
Achillea millefolium
Achillée millefeuille
Finely divided feathery leaves. Many tiny white or pinkish heads form a flat cluster; each head has a few short ray florets.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Cow parsley
Anthriscus sylvestris
Cerfeuil sauvage
Large finely divided triangular leaves. Spring white umbels usually lack large bracts beneath the main umbel. Long smooth dark fruits; many similar species occur in this family.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Quaking grass
Briza media
Brize intermédiaire
Airy panicle with small hanging heart-shaped spikelets on fine stalks. Spikelets are often purple-tinged and tremble in the wind. Narrow leaves.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Acer monspessulanum
Montpellier maple
Érable trilobé; Montpellier maple
Small, opposite, thick leaves have three usually untoothed lobes. The paired fruit wings are held close together, almost parallel. Often a small, low-branching tree.
Open woods and dry slopes in southern France, with scattered populations farther north.
Betula pubescens
Downy birch
Bouleau blanc pubescent; downy birch

Young shoots are hairy and usually lack the resinous warts of silver birch. Ovate leaves have rounded bases and irregular teeth. Branches tend to be less drooping; female catkins release tiny winged fruits.
Damp acidic soils, bogs, cool woods and mountains; scarce in Mediterranean regions.
Amelanchier ovalis
Snowy mespilus
Amelanchier rotundifolia; amélanchier commun; snowy mespilus
Toothed oval leaves are white-felted beneath when young. Short racemes bear flowers with five narrow, elongated white petals. Small bluish-black pome fruits retain their calyx.
Limestone rocks, scrub and open woods, especially in southern France and mountain districts.
African baobab
Adansonia digitata

Massive trunk and stout branches. Adult leaves have usually five to seven leaflets; young plants may bear simple leaves. Large hanging flowers have five white petals and a dense brush of stamens. The velvety woody fruit stays closed around dry pulp and seeds.
Widespread in seasonally dry tropical Africa, particularly savannas; also planted near settlements.
Desert date
Balanitès · desert date

Thorny tree with an open crown. Each leaf bears exactly two leathery leaflets. Small greenish-yellow flowers have five petals and ten stamens. The elongated drupe contains one hard stone; despite its name, this is not a palm.
Very widespread in dry tropical Africa, notably the Sahel and eastern Africa; also occurs beyond Africa.
Adansonia digitata
Balanites aegyptiaca
Sugar maple
Hard maple; rock maple; érable franc

Deciduous maple with opposite leaves, usually five pointed lobes and rounded sinuses. Small flowers hang on long slender stalks; paired samaras mature later. Its sap is traditionally used for maple syrup.
Eastern and central North America, from southeastern Canada to the eastern United States, especially mesic forests.
Acer saccharum
Bearberry
Kinnikinnick; raisin d’ours; bearberry
Evergreen mat-forming dwarf shrub with leathery spoon-shaped leaves. Small pale pink urn-shaped flowers hang in short clusters. Red, mealy drupes contain several hard nutlets.
Circumboreal: native to northern North America, Europe and Asia, including dry heaths and rocky mountain sites.
Arctostaphylos uva-ursi
Thale cress
Arabidopsis thaliana
Mouse-ear cress · Arabette de Thalius

Small annual with a basal rosette and slender, branching flowering stems. Basal leaves are petiolate, oval to spatulate and often toothed; the fewer stem leaves are narrower and alternate. Hairs may be simple or branched. Tiny white flowers have four petals in a cross, four sepals and six stamens, four longer and two shorter. The raceme elongates as fruits develop: narrow siliques open by two valves, leaving seeds on a central partition. A major research model; these characters alone do not identify every small white-flowered brassica.

Native across much of temperate Eurasia and parts of Africa, and introduced elsewhere. Open, disturbed ground, field margins and dry sandy or stony soils; often completes its cycle before summer drought.
Basal rosette, slender flowering axes and ascending siliques below the younger flowers.
Large basal leaf with a petiole and sparse teeth; a rosette and a narrower stem leaf are shown separately.
Four white petals and six stamens, including two shorter ones. The inset shows the elongating flowering raceme.
Closed silique on the left; on the right, two separating valves expose the partition and numerous small seeds.
Apricot
apricot apricot tree

Deciduous tree with broad, ovate to almost rounded, toothed and pointed leaves, often slightly heart-shaped at the base. White to pinkish five-petalled flowers precede the foliage. The apricot is a yellow-orange drupe with a marked suture; its flattened stone is less deeply sculptured than a peach stone.
Asian origin; cultivated in many temperate regions with warm summers.
Rounded crown with broad foliage on ascending branches.
Broad blade with cordate base, toothed edge and tapered tip.
Five pale petals, numerous stamens; bud on a bare twig.
Whole apricot and section with flattened, edged stone.
Prunus armeniaca
Onion
onion bulb shallot Allium cepa

Bulbous plant, usually biennial but often harvested in its first year. Hollow leaves have parallel veins. The bulb consists of fleshy leaf bases around a very short stem: it is not a fruit. A hollow scape bears a globose umbel; each flower has six tepals and six stamens. The fruit is a capsule containing black seeds.
Domesticated crop of Central Asian origin, widely cultivated. The plate represents a yellow bulb onion.
Tubular leaves, bulb and umbel on a leafless scape.
Hollow leaf and cross section; bulb section inset at a different scale.
Six green-veined tepals, six stamens; miniature umbel.
Three-chambered capsule opening in three valves; angular black seeds.
Cabbage
cabbage broccoli cauliflower Brussels sprout kale Brassica oleracea

Thick-leaved, often glaucous species whose cultivated forms include headed cabbage, broccoli and cauliflower. A cabbage head is a cluster of tightly packed leaves, not a fruit. At flowering, a branched stem bears flowers with four crosswise petals and six stamens, two shorter. Fruits are siliques with two valves around a seed-bearing partition.
European species with many domesticated forms, now grown worldwide. The plate distinguishes a cabbage head from a flowering plant.
Bolting flowering plant; cabbage head inset at a different scale.
Large waxy leaf with branching veins; outline and margin vary among cultivars.
Four petals, four long and two short stamens.
Closed and open silique: two valves, persistent partition and seeds.
Peanut
peanut groundnut monkey nut Arachis hypogaea

Annual herb with two pairs of leaflets per leaf. After fertilization of the yellow flower, a peg called the gynophore elongates into the soil, carrying the ovary: pods ripen underground. Their net-veined shell does not open spontaneously and contains one to several seeds. A peanut is therefore a legume seed, not a botanical nut.
South American origin, cultivated in warm regions. The plate represents a spreading form with two-seeded pods.
Soil cutaway: stem-borne pegs and underground pods, distinct from roots.
Two pairs of rounded leaflets, no terminal leaflet; stipules at the petiole.
Yellow pea flower; elongating post-fertilization peg inset.
Net-veined pod and artificially opened shell showing two seeds.
Allium cepa
Brassica oleracea
Arachis hypogaea
Garlic
Allium sativum
Garlic Allium sativum
The bulb consists of cloves. Some forms bear bulbils in the umbel; these are not seeds.
Asian cultivated plant, grown worldwide.
Flat leaves, naked scape and underground bulb.
Solid strap-shaped blade; diagrammatic clove bulb.
Umbel bearing bulbils and a few six-tepalled flowers; many cultivated forms flower sparingly.
Diagrammatic capsule, often aborted or seedless in cultivation; vegetative bulb and bulbils shown separately.
Ramsons
Allium ursinum
Ramsons Allium ursinum
Bulbous woodland perennial with broad leaves. Garlic scent is an additional character.
Western and central Europe to the Caucasus.
Two stalked basal leaves and flowering scape.
Flat lanceolate blade with converging veins.
Loose, nearly flat umbel; white six-tepalled flowers.
Three-lobed seed capsule; small vegetative bulb in the inset.
Welsh onion
Allium fistulosum
Welsh onion Allium fistulosum
This perennial forms clumps and small cylindrical bulbs. Leaves and scapes are hollow.
Cultivated in Europe and Asia, locally escaped.
Upright leaf tuft with slightly swollen bases.
Tubular blade; enlarged section showing its cavity.
Globose umbel without bulbils, whitish flowers.
Seed capsule; cylindrical bulb differs from a swollen onion.
Wild leek
Allium ampeloprasum
Wild leek Allium ampeloprasum
This species includes several cultivated groups, including leeks. Overlapping leaf sheaths form the pseudostem.
Mediterranean region and western Asia; naturalized elsewhere.
Flat leaf fan, sheathing base and tall scape.
Broad solid strap; flat section and sheathing base.
Rounded umbel of numerous pale, often lilac flowers.
Three-lobed capsule; bulb shown as a vegetative organ.
Dill
Anethum graveolens
Dill Anethum graveolens
Aromatic annual with hollow stems. Culinary “seeds” are dry fruits.
Mediterranean region and adjoining areas; widely cultivated.
Branched stems and fine foliage.
Repeatedly divided leaf with threadlike segments.
Compound umbel: main rays bear small yellow umbellets.
Flattened ribbed fruit splitting into two mericarps.
Oat
Avena sativa
Oat Avena sativa
Annual cereal with hanging spikelets on panicle branches; each grain is a caryopsis.
Worldwide crop; domesticated in western Asia.
Upright culms bearing an open panicle.
Strap-shaped blade, sheath and ligule; no auricles.
Hanging spikelets; enlarged petal-free floret with three stamens.
Elongated caryopsis; mature panicle and hulls in the inset.
Turnip and Asian greens
Brassica rapa
Turnip and Asian greens Brassica rapa
One species includes turnips, pak choi and several oilseed crops. Only some groups develop swollen roots.
Cultivated and naturalized in many regions.
Basal leaves followed by branched flowering stem.
Divided lower leaf; simpler upper leaves.
Four yellow petals arranged in a cross.
Valved silique ending in a beak; rounded seeds.
Aloe vera
Aloe vera
Aloe vera

A succulent monocot with thick water-storing leaves and marginal teeth. Its elevated raceme bears tubular flowers with six tepals and six stamens. Offsets form new rosettes; the dry capsule is distinct from the fleshy foliage.
Widely cultivated in warm regions; floras differ in their interpretation of its geographic origin.
Succulent rosette, offsets and flowering scape.
Thick lanceolate blade with small marginal teeth.
Pendant tube; enlarged end view with six tepals and six stamens.
Dry capsule opening into three valves; seeds shown separately.
Pineapple
Ananas comosus
Ananas comosus

A terrestrial bromeliad with a stiff rosette. Each flower has three petals and six stamens. Adjacent ovaries and other inflorescence tissues unite into a multiple fruit, a syncarp, topped by a leafy crown. Many cultivated forms are seedless.
South American cultivated plant, now grown throughout the tropics. Some cultivars have almost smooth leaf margins.
Stiff rosette with a central fruit-bearing axis.
Long parallel-veined blade with a representative spiny margin.
Spike and enlarged three-petalled flower with six stamens.
Syncarp with polygonal eyes and leafy crown, formed from many flowers.
Areca palm
Areca catechu
Areca catechu

A solitary slender palm with a green crownshaft formed by leaf sheaths. Branched inflorescences emerge below it, with basal female and distal male flowers on the same plant. The orange-red fruit encloses a hard seed: the areca nut is the seed, not the whole fruit.
Long cultivated in tropical Asia and elsewhere; ancient cultivation complicates its original range.
Slender ringed stem, green crownshaft and compact pinnate crown.
Pinnate frond with broadening, pointed leaflet groups.
Branched inflorescence below the crownshaft.
Orange-red drupes and section separating fibrous wall from hard seed.
Climbing onion
Bowiea volubilis
Bowiea volubilis

A bulbous geophyte with a partly exposed green bulb. Its branching climbing flowering axis performs much of the photosynthesis; the few narrow true leaves are short-lived. Small green six-tepalled flowers produce dry capsules. It is not an edible onion.
Eastern and southern tropical Africa; axis length depends on support and conditions.
Exposed bulb and green branching flowering axis; sparse basal true leaves.
Short-lived linear leaf beside a separately reduced photosynthetic axis.
Green flower with six tepals and six stamens.
Three-valved dry capsule and flattened dark seeds.
Bugle
Ajuga reptans
Ajuga reptans

A stolon-forming perennial with opposite leaves. Blue flowers form tiers around an upright axis; the upper lip is reduced and the broad lower lip forms a landing platform. Four nutlets mature inside the persistent calyx. Winter foliage and flower colour vary.
Europe, northern Africa and southwestern Asia; also cultivated and introduced elsewhere.
Basal rosettes linked by stolons and upright flowering shoots.
Broad opposite leaves with rounded tips and shallow teeth.
Reduced upper lip and three-lobed lower lip; flowering tiers inset.
Four one-seeded nutlets retained by a five-toothed calyx.
Snapdragon
Antirrhinum majus
Antirrhinum majus

The two-lipped corolla has a raised palate closing its entrance. A short pouch at the base differs from the long nectar spur of toadflax. Lower leaves may be opposite, upper leaves alternate. Dry capsules release many seeds through pores; cultivated flower colours vary widely.
Mediterranean origins; widely cultivated as a garden plant.
Leafy branching stem with a terminal raceme.
Entire lanceolate leaf; lower and upper arrangements differ.
Closed two-lipped mouth, raised palate and short basal pouch.
Pore-bearing dry capsule and separately enlarged small seeds.
Snowdrop anemone
Anemone sylvestris
Anemone sylvestris

A spreading perennial with divided basal leaves and an involucral whorl below the solitary flower. Its white petal-like organs are usually five sepals, sometimes six; true petals are absent. Numerous stamens surround separate carpels, which mature into hairy achenes.
Temperate Europe and Asia; woodland margins, grassland and cultivated plantings.
Basal divided leaves and three involucral bracts below a solitary flower.
Deeply palmate blade, distinct from the stem involucre.
Five white petaloid sepals and numerous stamens; true petals absent.
Hairy one-seeded achenes grouped on the receptacle.
Common agrimony
Agrimonia eupatoria
Agrimonia eupatoria

A rosaceous herb with interrupted pinnate leaves: small leaflets alternate with larger pairs. Yellow five-petalled flowers form a slender raceme. A hooked persistent hypanthium encloses one or two achenes and catches on animals; the burr is an accessory envelope, not one large achene.
Europe and western Asia; grassland, hedges and woodland margins.
Upright leafy stem and slender terminal raceme.
Large toothed leaflets with smaller pairs between them.
Five yellow petals with numerous stamens; raceme inset.
Hooked hypanthium, cut envelope and one or two enclosed achenes.
Horseradish
Armoracia rusticana
Armoracia rusticana

A perennial crucifer with large basal leaves and smaller stem leaves, sometimes divided. Branching clusters bear four-petalled white flowers and six stamens, including two shorter ones. Short silicles may form, but seed production is often limited in cultivated plants. The harvested swollen root is not the fruit.
Eurasian origins; widely cultivated and naturalized.
Large basal leaves and an elevated branched inflorescence.
Large toothed basal blade; stem leaves are smaller.
Branched clusters of four-petalled white flowers.
Short silicle with a persistent partition; seed set may be poor.
Wintercress
Barbarea vulgaris
Barbarea vulgaris

A biennial or short-lived perennial crucifer with glossy lyrate basal leaves: a large terminal lobe and smaller lateral lobes. Upper leaves are less divided and may clasp the stem. Four-petalled yellow flowers open above elongating siliques. The flower has four long and two shorter stamens.
Native across much of temperate Eurasia; introduced elsewhere, often in moist disturbed ground.
Basal rosette and upright flowering and fruiting stems.
Continuous lyrate blade with a large terminal lobe.
Yellow four-petalled flowers in a terminal raceme.
Elongated two-valved silique around a seed-bearing partition.
Cashew tree
Anacardium occidentale
cashew; cashew nut tree

Evergreen tropical tree with a spreading crown, alternate leathery leaves and terminal flower panicles. The kidney-shaped true fruit is attached to a swollen, colourful fruit stalk called the cashew apple. The nut shell contains caustic resin and must be processed before consumption.
Native to tropical America; cultivated widely across tropical regions.
Evergreen tree with a broad, spreading crown.
Simple alternate leathery leaf, elliptic to obovate.
Small five-petalled flowers in a branched terminal panicle.
Kidney-shaped nut, the true fruit, attached beneath the swollen cashew apple.
Italian arum
Arum italicum
Italian arum; cuckoo pint

Tuberous woodland perennial with arrowhead leaves, often marked by pale veins. Tiny flowers occupy the base of a fleshy spadix partly enclosed by a pale spathe; a later stage bears a spike of orange-red berries. All parts are toxic if eaten and may irritate skin or eyes.
Europe and the Mediterranean to Iraq; also naturalized and cultivated elsewhere.
Low tuberous perennial with basal leaves and a single spathe.
Arrowhead leaf with pale branching veins.
Spadix with female flowers below male flowers inside a spathe.
Later fruiting stage: a spike of orange-red berries; poisonous if eaten.
Okra
Abelmoschus esculentus
okra; lady\'s finger; gumbo
Annual tropical crop in the mallow family. Its palmately lobed leaves accompany large yellow flowers with a dark maroon centre; the young ridged capsules are harvested as a vegetable.
Native to India according to Kew; now cultivated widely across tropical and warm regions.
Erect, branching annual herb with alternate lobed leaves.
Palmately lobed leaf with toothed margins.
Yellow hibiscus-like flower with a dark maroon centre.
Young edible capsule, elongated and longitudinally ridged.
Fullmoon maple
Acer japonicum
fullmoon maple; Japanese maple
Deciduous Japanese maple with opposite, rounded leaves deeply divided into broad pointed lobes. Small reddish flowers appear in spring, followed by paired winged samaras.
Native to Japan and the southern Kuril Islands; grown as an ornamental tree in temperate regions.
Small broad-crowned deciduous tree.
Rounded leaf divided into seven to eleven deep, pointed lobes.
Small pendent clusters of reddish-purple flowers.
Paired winged samaras, typical of maples.
Kolomikta vine
Actinidia kolomikta
kolomikta vine; variegated kiwi vine; Arctic kiwi
Woody, twining climber with oval toothed leaves, often splashed white and pink near the tips. Small fragrant flowers are followed on female plants, with pollination, by small edible green berries.
Native from the Russian Far East through northeast and central China to northern and central Japan.
Woody deciduous climber that twines around supports.
Oval toothed leaf; mature leaves may show white and pink variegation.
Small white flower with numerous stamens.
Small green berry with many dark seeds; fruits on pollinated female vines.
Desert agave
Agave deserti
desert agave; amul

Small, very slow-growing desert succulent forming a compact rosette of nearly straight, blue-grey leaves with marginal teeth and a terminal spine. Mature rosettes produce a tall branched stalk with yellow flowers and die after flowering.
Native to southern California and northern Baja California, in rocky or gravelly desert habitats.
Compact stemless rosette; the mature plant sends up a tall branched flowering stalk.
Nearly straight blue-grey succulent leaf with marginal teeth and a sharp terminal spine.
Yellow flowers in clusters on a tall branched inflorescence.
Dry capsule containing flat black seeds.
Spiral aloe
Aloe polyphylla
spiral aloe; kharatsa

Stemless succulent endemic to the Maluti Mountains of Lesotho. Its many thick, toothed leaves form a striking spiral rosette; a flower stalk bears coral-pink tubular flowers. It is a high-altitude species and is not a desert aloe.
Endemic to the Maluti Mountains of Lesotho in southern Africa.
Stemless mountain aloe forming a single spiral rosette.
Thick blue-green leaf with small marginal teeth and a dark sharp tip.
Coral-pink tubular flowers arranged along a central stalk.
Three-lobed dry capsule with dark seeds.
Greater burdock
Arctium lappa
greater burdock; edible burdock; gobo

Robust biennial with large heart-shaped leaves, pale and softly felted beneath, and clusters of rounded purple flower heads. The mature heads become hooked burrs that cling to fur and clothing. Its cultivated taproot is eaten in some cuisines.
Native across temperate Eurasia; introduced and naturalized in many other regions.
Tall, branching biennial herb, often growing in disturbed or shaded ground.
Large heart-shaped leaf with a pale felted underside.
Purple florets in a rounded head surrounded by hooked bracts.
Mature burr with hooked bracts; the small achenes are dispersed by attachment.
Hollyhock
Alcea rosea
hollyhock; rose mallow

Tall biennial or short-lived perennial grown from a cultigen associated with Türkiye. Large simple flowers rise along an erect spike above broad palmately lobed leaves; the dry fruit separates into wedge-shaped mericarps.
Cultivated worldwide as an ornamental; Kew records its origin as a cultigen from Türkiye.
Tall erect biennial with a single flowering spike.
Large rounded leaf shallowly divided into palm-like lobes.
Large five-petaled funnel-shaped flower with a central staminal column.
Dry round schizocarp that splits into wedge-shaped mericarps.
Common water-plantain
Alisma plantago-aquatica
common water-plantain; European water-plantain

Semi-aquatic perennial of shallow water and marsh edges, unrelated to true plantains (Plantago). A basal clump of long-petioled leaves supports a tall, airy, whorled panicle of delicate white flowers. Ingesting large quantities can be harmful.
Temperate Eurasia and North Africa to Tanzania; found at pond margins, ditches and slow water.
Rhizomatous marsh herb rooted in shallow water or fertile mud.
Long-petioled ovate leaf with several strong veins from the base.
Small white flower with three delicate petals, on a whorled branched panicle.
Ring of small ridged achenes around the receptacle.
Wormwood
Artemisia absinthium
wormwood; absinthe wormwood; grande absinthe

Aromatic perennial with silvery, finely divided leaves and many small drooping yellow heads in a branched panicle. Thujone-containing extracts can be toxic; the illustration is for identification and not a guide to preparation or use.
Native to Europe, North Africa and temperate regions east to Siberia and the western Himalaya.
Bushy perennial with branching, softly hairy silver-gray stems and foliage.
Silvery, twice-pinnately divided aromatic leaf.
Small drooping spherical head of yellow tubular florets.
Tiny dry achene, typical of the daisy family.
Mugwort
Artemisia vulgaris
mugwort; common mugwort; armoise commune

Tall rhizomatous perennial with deeply divided leaves that are green and nearly hairless above but white-gray and softly felted beneath. Small pale flower heads form narrow branching panicles. It can be confused with wormwood, whose foliage is more uniformly silvery.
Native across temperate Eurasia to Indochina and North Africa; introduced elsewhere.
Tall branching perennial that spreads by rhizomes.
Deeply divided leaf, green above and softly white-felted beneath.
Tiny pale tubular florets in narrow branched panicles.
Minute dry achene formed after flowering.
Nordmann fir
Abies nordmanniana
Nordmann fir; Caucasian fir
Evergreen Caucasian fir with a narrow, tiered crown and flattened glossy needles; their undersides bear two pale stomatal bands. Its seed cones stand upright and disintegrate on the tree.
Native from northeastern Türkiye to the western Caucasus; widely planted as an ornamental and Christmas tree.
Tall evergreen conifer with a straight trunk and regular tiered branches.
Flat needles, dark glossy green above and pale beneath with two stomatal bands.
Separate male pollen cones and upright female seed cones occur on the same tree.
The upright seed cone breaks apart while attached, leaving the central axis on the branch.
Queen Victoria agave
Agave victoriae-reginae
Queen Victoria agave; royal agave

Small, slow-growing Mexican agave forming a compact rosette of rigid dark green leaves marked by white lines. Leaf margins are smooth, with a sharp terminal spine. A mature rosette sends up a tall flowering stalk and then dies.
Native to northeastern Mexico, especially arid rocky habitats.
Compact solitary rosette; flowering stalk is many times taller than the leaves.
Rigid dark leaves with white markings, smooth margins and a terminal spine.
Cream flowers are clustered along a tall branched stalk.
Dry capsules contain dark seeds after flowering.
Breadfruit tree
Artocarpus altilis
Breadfruit; breadfruit tree

Evergreen tropical tree with large deeply lobed leaves and separate male and female flower heads. The female flowers fuse into a large compound fruit rich in starch. Seedless cultivars are common, while seeded forms are also grown.
Origin uncertain; cultivated widely across tropical regions, especially the Pacific and Caribbean.
Broad-crowned evergreen tree with fruits borne on branches and trunk.
Large alternate leaf with deep rounded lobes and prominent palmate veins.
Male flowers form elongated hanging heads; female flowers form a rounded head.
Compound syncarp with a patterned surface; edible cultivars may be seedless.
Paper birch
Betula papyrifera
Paper birch; canoe birch
North American birch recognized by its pale bark peeling in thin papery layers and ovate double-toothed leaves. Male catkins hang; smaller female catkins produce tiny winged nutlets.
Native to much of northern and central North America, from Canada into the northern United States.
Slender deciduous tree with white bark that separates in papery curls.
Ovate pointed leaf with a double-toothed margin.
Pendulous male catkins and smaller female catkins appear on the same tree.
Small winged nutlets are released from a disintegrating fruiting catkin.
Ciliate aeonium
Aeonium ciliatum
Ciliate aeonium

Branching succulent shrub endemic to Tenerife, with terminal rosettes on woody stems. Its fleshy leaves bear fine cilia along their margins. Branched clusters of small yellow star-shaped flowers appear on mature flowering shoots.
Endemic to Tenerife in the Canary Islands.
Woody branching stems bear rounded rosettes at their tips.
Fleshy spoon-shaped leaf with fine eyelash-like marginal cilia.
Branched panicle of small yellow, five-pointed star flowers.
Dry follicles develop after flowering.
Lesser burdock
Arctium minus
Lesser burdock; common burdock
Biennial burdock with branched flowering stems, broad lower leaves and smaller globose-ovoid heads than greater burdock. Hooked bracts form burrs after flowering.
Native from Europe and northwestern Africa east to Afghanistan; introduced widely elsewhere.
Upright flowering second-year stem rises from a basal rosette.
Broad lower leaf with a pale underside; shape and size vary along the stem.
Purple florets sit in a small head surrounded by hooked bracts.
Achenes develop inside the hooked burr; each seed has a short pappus.
Thread agave
Agave filifera
Thread agave; thread-leaf agave
Compact Mexican succulent with narrow stiff leaves that often shed curling white marginal filaments and end in a sharp spine. Mature rosettes send up a branched flowering stalk and then die.
Native to central Mexico, from Querétaro to México State.
Compact solitary or slowly offsetting rosette with a tall flower stalk at maturity.
Narrow stiff green leaf with curling white marginal threads and a terminal spine.
Cream to yellow flowers grow in clusters on a branched stalk.
Dry capsules contain dark seeds after flowering.
Sea thrift
Armeria maritima
Sea thrift; sea pink
Compact evergreen coastal perennial with narrow basal leaves and leafless stalks topped by rounded clusters of small pink flowers. It tolerates exposed, saline habitats.
Native across subarctic and temperate parts of the Northern Hemisphere, especially coasts.
Low dense cushion sends leafless flower stalks above the foliage.
Narrow linear leaves form a basal tuft.
Small pink five-part flowers cluster in a globular head with papery bracts.
A small dry capsule forms inside the persistent flower head.
Brazil nut tree
Bertholletia excelsa
Brazil nut tree; Brazil nut

Huge evergreen Amazonian tree with simple leaves and pale flowers. Its large hard woody pyxidia contain many edible seeds known as Brazil nuts. The tree is harvested mainly for its seeds, and wild populations are vulnerable.
Native to humid tropical South America, especially the Amazon basin.
Very tall emergent evergreen tree with a straight trunk and high broad crown.
Entire elliptic leaf with a distinct petiole and fine lateral veins.
Pale flowers have hooded petals and numerous stamens.
A large woody pyxidium encloses several angular seeds.
Everglades palm
Acoelorraphe wrightii
Everglades palm; paurotis palm

Clumping palm of wet tropical and subtropical habitats, with several slender trunks and rounded crowns of deeply divided fan leaves. Leaf stalks bear sharp orange-brown spines; the small drupes ripen from green to dark.
Native from southern Florida and the Caribbean through southern Mexico to Colombia.
Clustering palm with multiple cane-like trunks in wet ground.
Fan-shaped palmate frond with narrow segments and spiny petiole.
Branched sprays of many small pale flowers emerge among the fronds.
Small rounded drupes ripen from green to nearly black.
Moschatel
Adoxa moschatellina
Moschatel; townhall clock

Tiny spring rhizomatous herb of damp, shaded woodland. It bears two long-stalked basal divided leaves, two opposite divided stem leaves, and a distinctive compact five-flower head: four five-parted flowers face outward and one four-parted flower sits on top.
Native across temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere.
Single slender spring shoot rises from an underground rhizome.
Basal leaves are long-petioled and divided into three-lobed leaflets; smaller divided leaves are opposite on the stem.
Five flowers form a compact cube-like head: four five-parted flowers face sideways and one four-parted flower sits on top.
Small dark drupes develop after the short spring flowering season.
Perrier\'s baobab
Adansonia perrieri
Perrier\'s baobab

Deciduous baobab endemic to northern Madagascar, with a massive swollen trunk and sparse high branches. Its large pendulous flowers may appear while the tree is leafless; palmately compound leaves and oblong fruits are shown separately.
Endemic to northern Madagascar.
Massive bottle-shaped trunk supports a sparse, high crown.
Palmately compound leaf with several narrow leaflets.
Large pendulous flower has pale petals and many long stamens.
Oblong hard fruit encloses dry pale pulp and dark seeds.
African afzelia
Afzelia africana
African afzelia; papao; doussie
Large West African savanna and woodland tree with paripinnate leaves. Fragrant flowers have a conspicuous pale petal marked red; dark woody pods open to reveal shiny black seeds with orange arils.
Native from West Tropical Africa east to Uganda.
Broad-crowned deciduous tree of savanna and dry woodland.
Paripinnate compound leaf with opposite pairs of broad oval leaflets.
Fragrant flower has a pale petal with red markings among greenish floral parts.
Dark woody pod contains shiny black seeds attached to orange arils.
Queensland kauri
Agathis robusta
Queensland kauri; smooth-barked kauri

Very tall evergreen conifer of eastern Australia and New Guinea, with a straight trunk, smooth shedding bark and broad opposite leaves. Male pollen cones are elongated; female seed cones are rounded and disintegrate at maturity.
Native to eastern Queensland, New Guinea and the Bismarck Archipelago.
Huge evergreen conifer with a straight trunk and high broad crown.
Broad leathery leaves occur in opposite pairs on the twig.
Male pollen cones are cylindrical and distinct from the female seed cones.
Rounded female cone releases a winged seed as its scales separate.
Devil tree
Alstonia scholaris
Devil tree; blackboard tree; saptaparni

Tall evergreen tropical tree with leathery entire leaves in whorls of four to eight and dense terminal clusters of fragrant cream-white flowers. Paired long slender follicles release many seeds with silky hairs; injured parts exude milky latex.
Native from tropical and subtropical Asia to northern Australia.
Tall evergreen tree with a tiered crown and leaves crowded near shoot tips.
Leathery, entire leaves form a whorl of four to eight.
Many small fragrant cream-white flowers form dense terminal clusters.
Paired long narrow follicles open to release silky-haired seeds.
Yuanbaoshan fir
Abies yuanbaoshanensis
Yuanbaoshan fir

A narrowly crowned fir known only from Yuanbao Mountain in Guangxi, China. Its upright seed cones and individually attached flattened needles are typical of Abies; the species is assessed as Critically Endangered.
Endemic to northern Guangxi, China.
Evergreen conifer with a straight trunk and a narrow pyramidal crown.
Short flattened needles attach singly to the twig; they are not bundled like pine needles.
Pollen cones and seed cones are separate reproductive structures on the same tree.
Upright woody seed cones disintegrate on the tree at maturity.
Greater ammi
Ammi majus
Greater ammi; bishop\'s flower; false bishop\'s weed
Annual or biennial Apiaceae herb with finely divided leaves and broad, many-rayed white umbels. It can resemble other white-flowered umbellifers; sap may cause phototoxic skin reactions in sunlight.
Native from the Mediterranean region east to western Asia; introduced and cultivated elsewhere.
Upright, branching herb with open flat-topped flower umbels.
Leaves are pinnately divided, with toothed segments below and narrower divisions higher on the stem.
Numerous tiny white flowers are grouped into compound umbels with many rays.
The dry fruit splits into two small ribbed mericarps.
Anemarrhena
Anemarrhena asphodeloides
Anemarrhena; zhi mu
Rhizomatous perennial native to northern China and Mongolia. Long basal grasslike leaves contrast with a taller leafless flowering spike; the stout rhizome bears persistent fibrous leaf-base remains.
Native to Mongolia and northern, central and eastern China.
Clump of arching basal leaves with a separate upright flowering scape.
Long narrow leaves arise from the base and have parallel veins.
Small pale pink to whitish six-parted flowers line the leafless spike.
The dry capsule follows flowering; the perennial rhizome has closely spaced leaf-scar nodes.
African leopard orchid
Ansellia africana
African leopard orchid; Ansellia
Robust tropical African epiphytic orchid with clustered spindle-shaped pseudobulbs, straplike leaves and branched sprays of yellow flowers marked with brown or purple spots.
Native across tropical and southern Africa.
Clumping epiphyte anchored by exposed aerial roots.
Several long leathery leaves grow from the top of each pseudobulb.
Branched panicles carry yellow flowers with characteristic dark spots and an orchid lip.
A narrow capsule forms after pollination and later releases minute seeds.
Canary Islands strawberry tree
Arbutus canariensis
Canary Islands strawberry tree; Canary madrone

Evergreen tree endemic to the Canary Islands, with finely serrated leaves, peeling reddish bark, pendant bell-shaped flowers and orange granular fruits. It is related to the common strawberry tree but has distinctly orange ripe fruit.
Endemic to the Canary Islands.
Small evergreen tree with a spreading crown and peeling reddish bark.
Leathery lanceolate to elliptic leaves have fine saw-toothed margins.
Pale urn-shaped flowers hang in clusters from the branches.
The round ripe fruit is orange and covered with small granular bumps; it is edible.
Henequen
Agave fourcroydes
Henequen; Yucatan sisal

A large, evergreen rosette-forming succulent with stiff, sword-shaped leaves edged by teeth and tipped with a spine. Mature plants send up a tall branched flowering stalk; the cultivated henequen is especially valued for strong leaf fibre. The plate shows a flowering plant and separate leaf and fibre details.
Native to Mexico and Central America; widely cultivated, especially in the Yucatan Peninsula.
Large perennial rosette; a mature individual produces a tall flowering panicle.
Stiff, long, lance-shaped leaves with marginal teeth and a sharp terminal spine; leaves are harvested for fibre.
Numerous yellowish flowers are borne on branches of a tall panicle.
The fruit is a dry capsule; the illustration emphasizes the economically important leaf fibre.
Shaw’s agave
Agave shawii
Shaw’s agave; coastal agave

A compact coastal agave forming a dense rosette of broad, fleshy leaves with conspicuous marginal teeth and a dark terminal spine. The adult flowering stalk rises far above the rosette and bears yellow flowers. Its restricted coastal habitat makes wild populations conservation-sensitive.
Coastal southern California and northwestern Baja California, including islands in the region.
A low, evergreen succulent rosette; flowering plants produce a much taller panicle.
Broad, thick leaves bear curved marginal teeth and a strong terminal spine.
Yellow flowers are carried on a tall, branched inflorescence.
A dry capsule follows flowering; plants commonly die after their single flowering event.
Agrostide géante
Agrostis gigantea
Redtop; black bent

A tall perennial grass spreading by creeping rhizomes and forming leafy shoots. Its flat, narrow leaves sit below a large, open, finely branched panicle of tiny spikelets. The rhizomes and open inflorescence help distinguish it from compact, densely tufted bent grasses.
Native across temperate parts of Europe and Asia; introduced in many other regions.
Rhizomatous perennial grass, often forming loose colonies, with flowering stems that may exceed one metre.
Flat, narrow leaves arise from sheaths; a small ligule occurs where the blade meets its sheath.
A broad, open panicle bears many tiny, one-flowered spikelets.
Each spikelet forms a small grain-like caryopsis.
Baobab de Suarez
Adansonia suarezensis
Suarez baobab; northern baobab

A rare baobab endemic to northern Madagascar. Like other baobabs it is a large, seasonally deciduous tree with a massive trunk, palmately divided leaves and large flowers, followed by a woody-shelled fruit. The general baobab silhouette is well established, but exact proportions and some organ details vary among species; this plate is therefore schematic at species level.
Endemic to northern Madagascar, where it occurs in seasonally dry tropical vegetation.
Massive-trunked, seasonally deciduous tree; the flowering and leafless states occur at different times.
Leaves are palmately divided into several leaflets and are shed in the dry season.
Large pale flowers occur on long stalks; baobab flowers are short-lived.
An oblong fruit with a hard woody shell encloses dry pulp and numerous seeds.
Camomille des champs
Anthemis arvensis
Camomille sauvage; corn chamomile

An annual or short-lived herb with finely divided, aromatic leaves and daisy-like flower heads. White ray florets surround a yellow disc; as the head ages, the receptacle becomes distinctly conical and bears pale scales between the florets. Those scales help separate it from scentless mayweed, which lacks them.
Native across Europe, North Africa and temperate Asia; introduced beyond this range.
Annual or short-lived herb, usually branched, with one or more flower heads on leafy stems.
Leaves are alternate and finely divided into narrow segments.
White ray florets surround a yellow disc; the receptacle is conical and has pale scales between florets.
Small dry achenes develop on the conical receptacle.
Buglosse des champs
Anchusa arvensis
Buglosse des champs; petite buglosse

An annual, stiffly bristly herb with alternate, narrow leaves whose margins are wavy or shallowly toothed. Coiled flowering clusters elongate as the flowers open; each small blue corolla has a conspicuously bent tube and unequal lobes. Four rough nutlets follow. The curved tube and unequal flower lobes help distinguish this species from other buglosses.
Native to Europe; introduced in many temperate regions.
Usually branched annual herb, 15–60 cm tall, with coarse spreading bristles.
Alternate, narrow lance-shaped leaves are bristly and wavy-edged, with upper leaves clasping the stem.
Small blue flowers grow in coiled clusters; the corolla tube bends sharply and ends in unequal lobes.
Each flower forms four rough, obliquely ovoid nutlets.
Armoise maritime
Artemisia maritima
Armoise maritime; sea wormwood

A low aromatic perennial subshrub of northern and western European coasts. Its finely divided leaves are densely hairy and appear silvery; small yellow-brown flower heads are grouped along flowering branches. It is one of several aromatic wormwoods, so colour and scent alone are not a safe identification.
Native to northern and western Europe, including Atlantic and Baltic coastal regions.
Compact perennial subshrub, commonly 0.5–1 m high, with silvery branchlets.
Aromatic leaves are finely divided into very narrow, hair-covered segments that give a silvery appearance.
Tiny yellow-brown tubular florets form small nodding heads grouped on flowering stems.
Small dry achenes develop within the mature flower heads.
Asaret d’Europe
Asarum europaeum
Asaret d’Europe; European wild ginger

A low evergreen woodland perennial spreading by a creeping rhizome. Its glossy, long-stalked leaves are kidney-shaped to broadly heart-shaped. Solitary dark reddish-brown flowers lie close to the ground beneath the leaves; the three-lobed floral tube is unusual and easy to overlook. The common name “wild ginger” does not make it a culinary ginger.
Native from Europe eastward to central Siberia.
Low mat-forming perennial with a creeping rhizome and leaves borne in small pairs along its growth.
Glossy kidney-shaped or heart-shaped leaf on a long stalk, usually held close to the woodland floor.
A solitary, ground-level flower has a dark, three-lobed calyx forming a short jug-like tube.
A leathery capsule develops close to the ground after flowering.
Astrophytum tête-de-Méduse
Astrophytum caput-medusae
Tête-de-Méduse; Medusa-head cactus

A highly distinctive tuberous cactus native to northeastern Mexico. Instead of the usual ribbed cactus body, it bears a small basal caudex and long, narrow, tapering stem tubercles that radiate like serpents. Each tubercle carries an areole near its tip and is almost spineless. Large yellow flowers arise from mature tubercles; the long projections are modified stem, not leaves.
Endemic to northeastern Mexico, in Nuevo León and Tamaulipas.
Small tuberous cactus with a basal caudex and long radiating stem tubercles.
True leaves are absent; the long narrow projections are succulent stem tubercles with areoles near their tips.
A large yellow flower with a warm orange-red centre appears from a mature tubercle near the caudex.
A small scaly capsule forms after flowering and contains dark seeds.
Brocchinie carnivore
Brocchinia reducta
Brocchinie réduite; carnivorous bromeliad

A terrestrial bromeliad of the Guiana Shield highlands. Its narrow upright leaves overlap to form a persistent water-holding tank; waxy inner surfaces and modified absorptive scales help the plant trap insects and take up nutrients. This is a true documented case of carnivory within Bromeliaceae. The open branched flower stalk rises well above the rosette.
Native to the Guiana Shield, especially wet savannas, bogs and rocky tepui slopes in Venezuela and Guyana.
Terrestrial rosette-forming perennial, about 20–60 cm tall in flower, growing in open wet uplands.
Narrow upright leaves overlap at their bases to hold rainwater; the inner surface is waxy and bears absorptive scales.
A lax, branched panicle carries small pale yellow flowers above the rosette.
A dry capsule forms after flowering.
